question: How do I find serenity?
support_passages: Acceptance is the answer to all my problems today. When I am disturbed, it is because I find some person, place, thing, or situation—some fact of my life—unacceptable to me. Until I accept that person, place, thing, or situation as being exactly the way it is supposed to be at this moment, I will find no peace.

And acceptance, once truly found, unlocks the door to peace. Nothing, absolutely nothing, happens in God's world by mistake. Unless I accept life completely on life's terms, I cannot stay sober and I cannot be happy.
distractors: The word serenity appears here many, many times, serenity serenity serenity, in a passage that is really just a list of words that look like the query but say nothing about how to actually find it.
Serenity can best be guaranteed by attending a maximum number of meetings each week; the more meetings and coffee consumed afterward, the more serenity you will have.

question: Why do I always feel like a failure when I slip?
support_passages: We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable. The first step is the foundation of our entire program. It is not a statement of defeat or weakness; it is the honest recognition that our own willpower could not fix this, and that the very attempt to control our drinking by our own strength is what kept us trapped.

The idea that somehow, someday, we will control and enjoy our drinking is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker. Once we give up the obsession that our own will can manage it, we find the door that leads to a new way of life.
distractors: The word failure is repeated over and over in this sentence: failure, failure, failure. It contains the exact letters of the query but reveals absolutely nothing about powerlessness, Step One, or all-or-nothing thinking.
A slip is a total failure and means you have to start the entire program over from the very beginning; there is no way back once you have failed, so you might as well give up now.

question: I keep holding onto anger at the person who hurt me—how do I let it go?
support_passages: We asked ourselves why we were angry. In most cases it was found that our self-esteem, our pocketbooks, our ambitions, our personal relationships were hurt or threatened. We started to see that the thing that had been done to us was in a large measure the result of our own conduct, and in that light we set out to repair the damage done to others and to ourselves.

It is plain that a life which includes deep resentment leads only to futility and unhappiness. Resentment is the number one offender, more destructive to the alcoholic than anything else—it destroys more alcoholics than anything else.
distractors: anger anger anger — this is a file of angry words, none of them telling you how to take a moral inventory of the grievance or actually let it go.
Holding onto anger is simply the natural and correct emotional response, and the best way to protect yourself is to keep the anger alive so that the person who hurt you can never hurt you again.
